lessonTitle: Sepsis: Early Warning Scores, the Initial Bundle and the Case for Cultures First

blocks.text: At 2 a.m. a healthcare assistant records a respiratory rate of 25 and a pulse of 118 on a post-operative patient and, three hours later, the same patient is confused with a blood pressure of 86 systolic. Each set of observations looked only a little worse than the last. A score that turns small, separate changes into a single number is what makes the deterioration impossible to overlook.

blocks.markdown: Sepsis is a time-critical emergency: mortality rises with delay to effective treatment. Early recognition depends on routine **physiological observations**, which are combined into an **early warning score (EWS)**. The score converts each vital sign into a weighted number and sums them; higher totals trigger more urgent clinical review. The example used here is based on the **National Early Warning Score 2 (NEWS2)** used in UK hospitals; exact scoring bands vary between systems and should be checked locally.

blocks.title: Early warning score
blocks.text: A track-and-trigger tool in which routine observations (respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, supplemental oxygen use, systolic blood pressure, pulse rate, level of consciousness and temperature) are each given 0 to 3 points, the points are summed, and the total (with any single extreme parameter) triggers a graded clinical response.

blocks.markdown: In this style of score, an aggregate of **0-4** is low risk (a single parameter scoring 3 prompts urgent ward-based review), **5-6** is medium risk and triggers urgent clinical review, and **7 or more** is high risk and triggers emergency assessment by a critical care or resuscitation-trained team. Any **new confusion** scores 3 on its own. The score identifies a **deteriorating** patient; it does not diagnose sepsis, so clinical judgement and a search for a source of infection are still required.

blocks.title: Scoring a patient
blocks.prompt: A patient has respiratory rate 24, oxygen saturation 93% on room air, systolic BP 98 mmHg, pulse 118, alert, temperature 38.6 degrees Celsius. Calculate the score and category.

steps.text: Respiratory rate 24 = 2; saturation 93% = 2; room air = 0; systolic 98 = 2; pulse 118 = 2; alert = 0; temperature 38.6 = 1.
A score of 7 or more is the high-risk band, requiring emergency assessment.

blocks.answer: Score 9: high risk; emergency response and a search for infection.

blocks.markdown: **The initial sepsis bundle.** A bundle is a short set of actions done together, ideally within the **first hour** of recognising sepsis. A widely taught version (the 'Sepsis Six') comprises three things to take and three to give: **take** blood cultures (and other cultures from the likely source), **measure serum lactate**, and **measure urine output**; **give** supplemental oxygen to maintain target saturation, **intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics**, and **intravenous fluid resuscitation**. For septic shock, vasopressors are added if blood pressure remains low after fluids, and the source is sought and controlled (for example drainage of an abscess). The urgency is greatest in septic shock, where each hour of delay in effective antibiotics is associated with higher mortality.

blocks.caption: Elements of an initial sepsis bundle
rows: Identify the organism and its susceptibilities
Marker of tissue hypoperfusion; guides severity and response
Marker of renal perfusion; low output suggests hypoperfusion
Cover likely organisms until culture results are available

blocks.markdown: **Why take blood cultures before antibiotics.** Antibiotics rapidly sterilise blood, so cultures taken **after** the first dose have a lower yield, which can leave the organism unidentified. A positive culture gives the **pathogen and its susceptibility pattern**, allowing therapy to be **narrowed or de-escalated** and unnecessary broad agents stopped, and informs the duration and source assessment. Good technique matters: two or more sets from separate venepunctures, adequate blood volume in each bottle, and careful skin antisepsis to reduce contamination. The cultures should not delay antibiotics in a critically ill patient: where taking them would cause a significant delay, antibiotics take priority.

blocks.title: Applying the bundle
blocks.prompt: A 66-year-old man with a high early warning score and suspected urinary sepsis arrives on the ward. Outline the order of the first actions.

steps.text: Recognise the high-risk score and call for senior or emergency help.
Take blood cultures and a lactate quickly and measure urine output, together with a urine sample for culture.
Without waiting for results, give oxygen if needed, intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics and intravenous fluids.
Reassess frequently; identify and control the source; review antibiotics when cultures return.

blocks.answer: Cultures, lactate and urine output taken rapidly, then oxygen, antibiotics and fluids within the first hour, with early review.

blocks.caption: A sustained output below about 0.5 mL/kg/h is a commonly used marker of reduced renal perfusion

items: Early warning scores add weighted vital signs to detect deterioration early.
A high score triggers emergency review; it does not itself diagnose sepsis.
Bundle: cultures, lactate, urine output, oxygen, antibiotics, fluids.
Cultures before antibiotics improve yield and enable de-escalation, but must not delay treatment.

blocks.title: Time matters
blocks.text: Delay in effective antibiotics and source control is associated with increased mortality in septic shock. The bundle is designed so that the key actions happen together and quickly.

blocks.title: Scores are aids, not replacements for judgement
blocks.text: Patients on beta-blockers may not become tachycardic, older patients may not be febrile, and a low score with a worried clinician still needs review. Local protocols and score variants differ.

points: Early warning scores sum weighted vital signs and trigger graded responses; a higher score means greater risk.
The initial bundle takes cultures, lactate and urine output and gives oxygen, antibiotics and fluids.
Blood cultures are taken before antibiotics (if no delay) because antibiotics reduce yield, and results allow targeted therapy and de-escalation.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of an early warning score?

options.text: To combine routine vital signs into a number that identifies a deteriorating patient and triggers a graded response
To identify the causative organism
To select the antibiotic dose
To confirm sepsis without clinical assessment

questions.correctOptionText: To combine routine vital signs into a number that identifies a deteriorating patient and triggers a graded response

distractorRationale.d: Scores aid recognition but do not replace clinical assessment.

questions.explanation: Early warning scores turn small changes in several observations into a single trigger. They flag deterioration but do not by themselves diagnose sepsis.

questions.stem: Using the NEWS2-style table in this unit, which patient has the highest total score?

options.text: Respiratory rate 26, saturation 90% on oxygen, systolic 88, pulse 128, confused, temperature 39.4
Respiratory rate 14, saturation 98% on air, systolic 125, pulse 72, alert, temperature 37.0
Respiratory rate 22, saturation 95% on air, systolic 112, pulse 92, alert, temperature 37.8
Respiratory rate 18, saturation 96% on air, systolic 105, pulse 88, alert, temperature 36.5

questions.correctOptionText: Respiratory rate 26, saturation 90% on oxygen, systolic 88, pulse 128, confused, temperature 39.4
questions.explanation: Summing the parameter scores shows option a scores 18, the most severe by far. The others are normal or only mildly abnormal.

questions.stem: Which pair lists two elements of an initial sepsis bundle?

options.text: Serum lactate measurement and intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics
Chest physiotherapy and dietary assessment
Urinary catheter removal and nutritional supplements
Oral antibiotics and bed rest

questions.correctOptionText: Serum lactate measurement and intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics

distractorRationale.b: These are not part of the initial bundle.
distractorRationale.c: Not part of the initial bundle.
distractorRationale.d: Intravenous, not oral, antibiotics are used in sepsis.

questions.explanation: The bundle includes cultures, lactate, urine output, oxygen, intravenous antibiotics and intravenous fluids. They are delivered together within the first hour.

questions.stem: A patient with septic shock has had three litres of fluid but remains hypotensive with a lactate of 5.0 mmol/L. Which additional step is part of the sepsis management approach described?

options.text: Start vasopressors to maintain a mean arterial pressure of at least 65 mmHg and look for a source to control
Stop antibiotics until cultures are available
Remove all oxygen
Discharge with oral therapy

questions.correctOptionText: Start vasopressors to maintain a mean arterial pressure of at least 65 mmHg and look for a source to control

distractorRationale.c: Oxygen is part of the bundle.
distractorRationale.d: The patient requires urgent critical care.

questions.explanation: Persistent hypotension after fluid resuscitation defines septic shock, for which vasopressors are used. Source control, such as drainage, is also needed.

questions.stem: Why should blood cultures be taken before the first dose of antibiotics, when this causes no significant delay?

options.text: Antibiotics quickly sterilise the blood, reducing culture yield and the chance of identifying the organism and its susceptibilities
Blood cultures make antibiotics work faster
Cultures taken after antibiotics always show resistant organisms
Cultures are only valid if the patient is afebrile

questions.correctOptionText: Antibiotics quickly sterilise the blood, reducing culture yield and the chance of identifying the organism and its susceptibilities

distractorRationale.b: Cultures do not affect antibiotic action.
distractorRationale.c: Cultures after antibiotics usually show no growth, not resistance.
distractorRationale.d: Cultures are taken during fever and before treatment.

questions.explanation: Once antibiotics are in the bloodstream, viable organisms may no longer grow in the bottle. Identifying the organism allows narrowing of therapy later.

questions.stem: A patient has respiratory rate 26 (3 points), oxygen saturation 95% (1 point) on supplemental oxygen (2 points), systolic BP 104 mmHg (1 point), pulse 104 (1 point), new confusion (3 points) and temperature 37.2 degrees Celsius (0 points). Add the points to give the total early warning score.
questions.explanation: The total is 3 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 3 + 0 = 11. A score of 7 or more falls in the high-risk band requiring emergency assessment.

questions.stem: A 75 kg patient with suspected sepsis passes 120 mL of urine over 4 hours after a catheter is placed. Calculate the urine output in mL/kg/h, and note that sustained output below about 0.5 mL/kg/h suggests reduced renal perfusion. Give your answer in mL/kg/h.
questions.explanation: Urine output = 120 / (75 x 4) = 120 / 300 = 0.4 mL/kg/h. This is below 0.5 mL/kg/h, consistent with reduced renal perfusion and an indicator of sepsis-related organ dysfunction.

questions.stem: Explain how an early warning score is used to identify a deteriorating septic patient, and give two limitations of relying on the score alone.
markingGuide: Weighted scores for respiratory rate, saturation, oxygen use, systolic BP, pulse, consciousness and temperature are summed
Higher totals (and a single extreme parameter) trigger graded escalation, such as urgent or emergency review
Repeated observations detect trends and small changes that would otherwise be missed
Limitation: does not diagnose infection or sepsis; clinical assessment still needed
Limitation: false reassurance in beta-blocked, elderly or immunosuppressed patients, and variation between score versions
questions.explanation: Scores structure escalation and make deterioration visible. They support but do not replace clinical judgement.

questions.stem: List the elements of an initial sepsis bundle and state why it is delivered in the first hour.
markingGuide: Early treatment is associated with better outcomes, particularly in septic shock; vasopressors and source control as needed
questions.explanation: The bundle groups time-critical actions so that none are forgotten. The first hour matters because mortality rises with delay to effective therapy.

questions.stem: Explain why blood cultures should be taken before antibiotics in suspected sepsis, and when this principle should not be applied.
markingGuide: Antibiotics reduce the chance of growing the organism, lowering culture yield
Positive cultures identify the pathogen and its susceptibilities
Results allow targeted therapy and de-escalation or stopping broad agents
Technique: separate venepunctures, adequate volume, skin antisepsis to limit contamination
Exception: if obtaining cultures would cause a significant delay in a critically ill patient, antibiotics take priority
questions.explanation: Culture yield falls once antibiotics are given, and the result guides the rest of treatment. Patient safety overrides the sequence if cultures would delay treatment.
